source.subject: Biology
source.unit: Unit 1 — Diversity in the Living World
source.source_scope: Only the content printed on PDF page 8: Chordata and plant Division; kingdoms Animalia and Plantae; ascending taxonomic hierarchy, sub-categories and common-character trends; Table 1.1 entries for man, housefly, mango and wheat.

questions.question: Which two features are mentioned on this page as common features supporting placement in phylum Chordata?
options: Notochord and dorsal hollow neural system
questions.explanation: The page names the notochord and dorsal hollow neural system as common features for this placement.
questions.source_text: presence of notochord and dorsal hollow neural system, are included in phylum Chordata

questions.question: What is the higher category called when plant classes with a few similar characters are grouped together?
questions.explanation: The passage states that in plants, the higher category is called Division.
questions.source_text: In case of plants, classes with a few similar characters are assigned to a higher category called Division.

questions.question: Which organisms are assigned to Kingdom Animalia in the classification system described?
questions.explanation: The page says all animals belonging to various phyla are assigned to Kingdom Animalia.
questions.source_text: All animals belonging to various phyla are assigned to the highest category called Kingdom Animalia

questions.question: What does Kingdom Plantae comprise according to the page?
questions.explanation: The passage says Kingdom Plantae comprises all plants from various divisions.
questions.source_text: The Kingdom Plantae, on the other hand, is distinct, and comprises all plants from various divisions.

questions.question: Which taxonomic category is described as the highest category in the animal classification system?
questions.explanation: The page calls Kingdom Animalia the highest category in animal classification.
questions.source_text: the highest category called Kingdom Animalia in the classification system of animals

questions.question: Which taxonomic category is at the bottom of Figure 1.1, with the hierarchy ascending toward kingdom?
questions.explanation: Figure 1.1 shows species at the bottom and kingdom at the top in ascending order.
questions.source_text: shown in ascending order starting with species in Figure 1.1

questions.question: Which sequence correctly follows the ascending order shown in Figure 1.1?
options: Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum/Division → Kingdom
Kingdom → Species → Genus → Class → Family → Order
Species → Family → Genus → Kingdom → Order → Class
questions.explanation: The figure lists the categories from species upward to kingdom in this order.
questions.source_text: Kingdom; Phylum or Division; Class; Order; Family; Genus; Species

questions.question: Why have taxonomists developed sub-categories within the hierarchy, according to the page?
options: To facilitate more sound and scientific placement of taxa
To make all organisms members of one genus
To replace species with local names
questions.explanation: The passage says sub-categories help place taxa more soundly and scientifically.
questions.source_text: taxonomists have also developed sub-categories in this hierarchy to facilitate more sound and scientific placement of various taxa.

questions.question: As one moves upward from species to kingdom, what happens to the number of common characteristics?
options: It becomes zero at species level
questions.explanation: The page explicitly says common characteristics decrease higher up the hierarchy.
questions.source_text: as we go higher from species to kingdom, the number of common characteristics goes on decreasing.

questions.question: Members within a lower taxon share:
options: Fewer characteristics than every higher taxon
questions.explanation: The passage states that lower taxa share more characteristics among their members.
questions.source_text: Lower the taxa, more are the characteristics that the members within the taxon share.

questions.question: According to the page, why is it harder to determine relationships among taxa at the same level in higher categories?
options: There are fewer common characteristics to guide comparison
Higher taxa contain only one organism
All higher taxa have identical characters
Their scientific names are not available
questions.explanation: The text links higher categories with fewer common characteristics and greater difficulty determining relationships among taxa at the same level.
questions.source_text: Higher the category, greater is the difficulty of determining the relationship to other taxa at the same level.

questions.question: What happens to the problem of classification as taxonomic categories become higher, according to the page?
options: It becomes simpler in every case
It becomes only a naming problem
questions.explanation: The passage concludes that classification becomes more complex at higher categories.
questions.source_text: Hence, the problem of classification becomes more complex.

questions.question: Which organisms are compared in Table 1.1 for their taxonomic categories?
questions.explanation: Table 1.1 lists man, housefly, mango and wheat.
questions.source_text: some common organisms like housefly, man, mango and wheat

questions.question: Which genus and family are listed for Man in Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: The table gives Homo as genus and Hominidae as family for Man.
questions.source_text: Man Homo sapiens Homo Hominidae Primata Mammalia Chordata

questions.question: Which order is listed for the housefly in Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: The housefly row lists Diptera under Order.
questions.source_text: Housefly Musca domestica Musca Muscidae Diptera Insecta Arthropoda

questions.question: Which family is listed for mango in Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: The table lists Anacardiaceae as the family for mango.
questions.source_text: Mango Mangifera indica Mangifera Anacardiaceae Sapindales Dicotyledonae Angiospermae

questions.question: Which genus is listed for wheat in Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: The wheat row lists Triticum as the genus.
questions.source_text: Wheat Triticum aestivum Triticum Poaceae Poales Monocotyledonae Angiospermae

questions.question: Which Phylum/Division entry is listed for both mango and wheat in Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: Both mango and wheat rows show Angiospermae in the Phylum/Division column.
questions.source_text: Mango ... Angiospermae; Wheat ... Angiospermae

questions.question: Which organism-to-order matches are correct according to Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: Table 1.1 lists Primata for man, Diptera for housefly, Sapindales for mango and Poales for wheat.
questions.source_text: Man ... Primata; Housefly ... Diptera; Mango ... Sapindales; Wheat ... Poales

questions.question: Which organism-to-class matches are shown in Table 1.1?
questions.explanation: These are the class entries printed in the table for the four organisms.
questions.source_text: Mammalia; Insecta; Dicotyledonae; Monocotyledonae
